How it works

  1. 1SensePhone accelerometer, about 60 samples per second. Turning is read from how the direction of gravity changes.
  2. 2Window0.25 s averages that keep their peaks, grouped into 2 s windows every 0.5 s, 7 features each.
  3. 3Modelk-nearest neighbours names the activity, smoothed so it does not flicker, and flags motion it has never seen.
  4. 4DoseImpact peaks and squat time turn into two daily scores.
  5. 5AdviseBehind pace: suggests jumping or resistance work, with how much.

The built-in model learned rest, walking and squats from recordings of a worn sensor. Running and jumping are simulated until real recordings exist. Use the calibrate buttons to retrain it on your own phone. The gyroscope is not used, because the training sensor has none.

What the NASA bone data says

  • MR035G DXA scans, Campaign 3 bed rest: hip bone density fell 2.59% on average when load was removed (17 subjects with hip scans).
  • MR079G strength change vs hip bone change: ρ = 0.41, p = 0.10. A faint trend, not proven.
  • NASA's public archive has no exercise-dose or impact records, so the loading targets here are heuristics. NASA's data-request portal lists ARED, Force_Shoes and vertical-jump records that would calibrate them.

03What the model suggests

Rule-based

    The activity model names what you did. Simple rules compare it with the daily targets. The exercise amounts are starting suggestions, not prescriptions.

    04Tomorrow's targets

    Experimental
    GoalTodayTargetHow

    Wear the phone in the same spot every day so the numbers are comparable. Targets are prototype values.

    05Bone density scans

    Clinical measurement (DXA)

    The app does not measure bone density. A DXA scan does. Enter your last two scans to track the change next to your loading.

    Saved on this phone only. For comparison, NASA bed-rest Campaign 3 (MR035G) averaged a 2.59% fall in hip density. If your scans show a drop, talk to your doctor or flight surgeon. The app cannot diagnose.

      Safety and limitations

      • One phone on the knee measures impact size and time since the last strong impact. Activity type and the two loading scores are model estimates and heuristics.
      • The built-in model learned rest, walking and squats from one person wearing a logger, and running and jumping are simulated. Recording each movement on your own phone retrains it.
      • The scores are loading activity, not bone density. Only a DXA scan measures bone density, and the app cannot diagnose.
      • A phone is much heavier than a sensor pod, so pull the strap extra tight. A loose phone bounces and records fake impacts.
      • Phone web pages expose acceleration and rotation only, not infrared or other sensors, and the classifier uses acceleration only. Sensors stop when the phone locks.
      • Sensing and the model run on the phone. Nothing is uploaded.

      Troubleshooting

      • No motion data arrives. Open this page directly in Safari or Chrome over https, not inside another app, and allow motion access. Demo mode still works.
      • Motion access was denied. Quit Safari fully, reopen the page and tap Allow. If it still fails, clear the data for this site in Settings, Apps, Safari, Advanced, Website Data.
      • The page is inside a frame. iPhone Safari blocks the motion sensors there. Open the page directly.
      • The stand-still check fails. Hold still, tighten the strap and run it again.
      • Unrecognized motion alert. Recalibrate on your own phone, or check the strap.
      NASA Space Apps Challenge · New York · 2026

      Did today's workout protect your bones?

      BoneLoad turns the phone strapped to an astronaut's knee into a bone loading monitor. It tells the crew through the day whether their movement loaded the skeleton enough, and what to do if it didn't.

      Open the monitorSetup guide
      ~1 to 1.5%bone mass lost per month in hips and spine (approx.)
      1 phoneon the knee, no extra hardware to start
      5 minutessetup, then it runs all day
      1/6 gMoon gravity: walking loads bone far less

      Exercise only protects bone if it loads it hard enough

      Our challenge, Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions, names bone density loss as one of the hazards crews must spot and act on themselves.

      Bone needs force, not minutes

      Bone responds to peak force and how fast it rises. A few hard, fast reps beat many easy ones, but nobody tells astronauts which kind they just did.

      The Moon makes it worse

      At 1.62 m/s², walking on the lunar surface loads the skeleton about 1/6 as much as on Earth. Crews will need targeted exercise to make up the gap.

      Houston is far away

      With communication delays, the crew needs the answer on board, right after the workout, with clear next steps.

      How it works

      An accelerometer feels every force except gravity, so a phone on the leg feels every impact the skeleton takes.

      1. 1SenseThe phone's accelerometer is read in the browser at about 60 samples per second. Nothing leaves the phone. A 3 second stand-still check confirms the sensor and strap.
      2. 2ProcessThe signal is averaged in 0.25 second steps that keep their peaks, then grouped into 2 second windows every 0.5 seconds.
      3. 3ClassifyA k-nearest-neighbours model reads each window, names the activity, and is smoothed so it does not flicker.
      4. 4EstimateImpact peaks and squat time turn into two daily scores.score = 100 · (1 − e−dose/D)
      5. 5RecommendA status of On pace, Watch or Behind, with advice such as “about 70 more hops or heel drops” or “3 more minutes of squats”, and alerts for hard impacts and long stretches with no strong impact.

      Methodology

      What the prototype does with the signal, and where its assumptions are.

      StageWhat it doesStatus
      AccelerometerRead from the phone in the browser at about 60 samples per second. Turning is worked out from how the direction of gravity changes.measured
      Signal processing0.25 s averages that keep their peaks, grouped into 2 s windows every 0.5 s, 7 features per window.measured
      Activity classificationk-nearest neighbours over those features, smoothed so it does not flicker, with a novelty check for motion it has never seen. The built-in set is real recordings of rest, walking and squats from one person wearing a 3-axis logger, plus simulated running and jumping. Calibration on your own phone replaces it.small real + simulated data
      Impact detectionPeaks above 2 g are counted, and only while the model says walking, running or jumping.measured
      Loading estimationBigger peaks count more and each extra impact counts less. Resistance loading is the time classified as squat or lift. Target: a score of 60 by the end of the day.heuristic

      The prototype is not a validated clinical prediction system. Loading scores describe activity, not bone mineral density, which only a DXA scan measures.

      Live simulation

      Watch slow squats barely move the score, then jump squats fill it. Switch to the Moon to see the same workout lose most of its load. Simulated data, same physics as our analysis code. This is the full three-sensor concept (pelvis, knee, ankle) the team is building toward. The Monitor tab runs the one-phone version.

      Hardware

      One pod design on an adjustable velcro strap fits almost anyone. Accelerometer and phone modules share the same dovetail clip, or stick straight onto the strap with velcro.

      Phone-only today

      The monitor needs one phone strapped just above the kneecap. A phone is heavier than a sensor pod, so pull the strap extra tight or it records fake impacts.

      Calibrate once, wear one

      In the full system a weekly 5-minute session with all three sensors teaches the app each person's leg. Every other day, the pelvis sensor alone predicts the rest.

      Accelerometers only

      Force, femur load, impacts, jump height and balance need no gyroscope. Gyros later unlock fast joint angles and neck torques.

      Flight version

      In orbit, slow resistance exercise barely accelerates the body, so the flight design adds in-line load cells on the treadmill harness.

      What we measure today, and what comes next

      We measure the loading that goes into the skeleton. Stress inside bone needs scans and musculoskeletal models, so we don't claim it.

      1. BuiltKnee phone acceleration and on-device activity model
      2. BuiltDaily impact and resistance loading score with advice, with heuristic targets
      3. SimulationGround force and bone loading score from the pelvis, built in the simulation
      4. In progressFemur and knee loads from three sensors
      5. FutureTargets calibrated on NASA exercise-dose records (ARED, Force_Shoes), which need a NASA data request
      6. FutureNeck module: astronauts had cervical disc herniations at 21.4 times the control rate, cause unknown. Needs a head sensor with a gyroscope.
      7. FutureMuscle and joint contact forces (musculoskeletal modeling)
      8. FutureStress inside bone (needs CT or MRI geometry)

      Built by Team BoneLoad at NASA Space Apps Challenge, New York, November 14 to 15, 2026. Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.
